# Bazaar Commerce — full index for language models

Open-source multi-vendor marketplace engine for cash-on-delivery markets.
Apache-2.0. Maintained by Cubitrek. https://github.com/Cubitrek/bazaar-commerce

Built on MedusaJS 2.18 and Mercur 2.3, in TypeScript, with PostgreSQL and Redis.

--------------------------------------------------------------------------------
THE PROBLEM
--------------------------------------------------------------------------------

Standard ecommerce software models one money flow: authorize a card, capture it,
pay the seller. In Pakistan, Bangladesh, Egypt, Nigeria and much of South and
Southeast Asia roughly 95% of orders are cash on delivery, which breaks that at
every step:

- There is no authorization, so there is nothing to capture.
- The money arrives days later, from a courier rather than the buyer.
- It arrives in a batch covering many orders, sometimes short.
- Between 20% and 40% of parcels are returned to origin undelivered, and the
  seller pays freight in both directions.
- Stripe Connect does not serve businesses registered in many of these markets,
  so the standard payout module is unusable regardless of cost.

The money path therefore cannot hang off the payment lifecycle. It hangs off
courier remittance, which is a separate, slower and messier timeline. That single
decision explains most of the architecture.

--------------------------------------------------------------------------------
MODULES
--------------------------------------------------------------------------------

settlement            packages/api/src/modules/settlement
  Double-entry ledger. Accounts: cod_receivable, psp_clearing, bank,
  seller_payable, commission_revenue, sales_tax_payable,
  withholding_tax_payable, settlement_loss. Every write must balance and is
  idempotent on a business-fact key. Remittance lines match on airway bill;
  short payments, unknown AWBs, duplicates and overdue remittances become
  explicit exceptions rather than silent adjustments.
  Load-bearing decisions: placement posts nothing; a mismatched remittance is a
  dispute not an adjustment; collected-but-unremitted cash is not payable.

order-confirmation    packages/api/src/modules/order-confirmation
  Holds a parcel until the buyer confirms. State machine: pending, contacted,
  escalated, then confirmed or cancelled. Only confirmed releases dispatch,
  enforced in API middleware so the vendor app and connectors cannot route
  around it. Risk scoring is a pure function over payment method, buyer history,
  order value, address quality and basket size.
  Load-bearing decisions: silence is not refusal except in the high-risk band,
  because most buyers ignore messages and cancelling quiet buyers destroys more
  good orders than the returns it prevents; the gate fails OPEN.

digital-fulfilment    packages/api/src/modules/digital-fulfilment
  Encrypted vault of sellable codes plus a delivery ledger. AES-256-GCM under a
  key separate from the session secret. Allocation is a single atomic statement
  using FOR UPDATE SKIP LOCKED. Fraud gate scores velocity, buyer verification,
  distinct top-up targets and first-purchase value.
  Load-bearing decisions: the gate fails CLOSED, because a released code cannot
  be recalled; refusal requires evidence of fraud rather than absence of trust;
  refundability turns on whether the buyer has seen the code.

payout-pakistan       packages/api/src/providers/payout-pakistan
  Implements Mercur's four-method IPayoutProvider behind a driver interface.

--------------------------------------------------------------------------------
DOCUMENTED TRAPS
--------------------------------------------------------------------------------

Each of these produced a plausible wrong answer rather than an error.

1. order.total is computed from whichever item fields were requested. Asking for
   items.id reported a PKR 156,050 order as PKR 250. Request items.* or no item
   fields at all.
2. order_line_item.total is not a column. Inside an order.placed subscriber it
   reads 0 while unit_price holds the real figure.
3. Mercur emits ONE order.placed carrying an ARRAY of {id}, one per seller.
4. Medusa creates a customer row for guest checkouts, so customer_id does not
   distinguish a guest. Only customer.has_account does.
5. Mercur hardcodes requires_shipping: true on every cart line item.
6. listProductCategories omits name unless select is passed.
7. Commission rules match a product's DIRECT categories only; no ancestor walk.
8. Workflow hook handlers must return a StepResponse; a plain object is silently
   discarded.
9. Medusa substitutes a fake Redis if REDIS_URL is unset.

--------------------------------------------------------------------------------
VERIFICATION
--------------------------------------------------------------------------------

229 assertions across seven suites, run from packages/api:

  test:settlement    34    COD ledger, courier reconciliation, tax split
  test:payout        26    payout provider and Mercur wiring
  test:csv           34    catalogue import validation
  test:shopify       29    token rotation, throttling, HMAC verification
  test:otp           22    brute force, SMS pumping, expiry
  test:confirmation  40    RTO risk bands, dispatch gate, token handling
  test:digital       44    encryption, concurrent allocation, fraud gate

Every suite was proven able to fail by deliberately breaking the code it covers.
Two end-to-end smoke tests drive a real cash-on-delivery order and a real digital
purchase against a running stack.

--------------------------------------------------------------------------------
STATUS
--------------------------------------------------------------------------------

Pre-production. The engine is verified; the commercial integrations are not,
because they need contracts rather than code: no payment provider (payouts use a
mock driver), no SMS or WhatsApp gateway (messages print to the console), no
courier contract (remittance formats modelled from specifications).

Two defects are open and documented in docs/known-issues.md, including a
free-shipping leak on physical products.
